The remaining three are written down here as the standing queue for the last three days before the
24th, in priority order. Nothing below is started today unless the item above lands early.

## Work log

<!-- Chronological, written as you go. What was actually done, why, what it cost.
     Reference commits and link to plans and notes. Prose beats a checklist here —
     this is the part you will actually reread in three months. -->

- **Measured the problem before designing for it.** 19.31 MB raw / 4.42 MB gzipped, 68,704
  buildings, 317,927 footprint vertices at a mean of 4.63 each, ~997k triangles. All of the
  triangles are buildings: roads are already a canvas texture and water and green are a few
  hundred flat polygons. So there was only ever one thing to cut.
- **"For phones we can have a prerendered cityscape so it's just an image no?"** — asked
  mid-session, and the answer turned out to be better than a workaround. `Diorama.tsx` sets
  `enableRotate={false}` on an orthographic camera, so **zooming is exactly a 2D scale of the
  projected image and panning is exactly a 2D translation**. A pre-rendered cityscape is not a
  lossy stand-in for the geometry — it is the same picture, and only resolution degrades.

  Where it wins: at district fit the whole 47 km² is 1,076 × 621 px on a phone. Where it fails:
  at block fit the same extent needs 1.07 Gpx on a phone and 6.5 Gpx on the laptop — a tile
  pyramid, i.e. rebuilding a slippy map. So an image answers the district register completely and
  the block register not at all.
- **`docs/roadmap.md` had already rejected pre-rendered raster** under *Device reach*: it "needs
  hand-maintained hit regions, an image set per scenario and zoom level, and hotspot coordinates
  kept in sync by hand". That objection is about who maintains the image, not about whether it is
  correct — generated from the scene document, all three derive and cannot drift. The roadmap's
  own preferred alternative ("render the same scene document to SVG or Canvas 2D with a
  painter's-algorithm isometric projection") is exactly the generator that got built.
- **Chose the hybrid**: geometry where there is content, raster where there is context — the
  hero/stock distinction `Buildings.tsx` already draws, pushed one step further.
  `plans/2026-09-21_backdrop-lod.plan.md`.
- **`lod.ts`** — the partition, 23 tests. At 1,250 m: 7,588 buildings / 112k triangles stay
  geometry (budget is 100–150k), 61,116 / 885k go to the backdrop. The radius is a proxy and says
  so; the real rule is that heroes are always geometry at any distance, so item 5's content takes
  over from distance without a code change. One contract question surfaced in test: a building
  whose centroid sits exactly on the centre survived `radiusM: 0`, so a non-positive radius now
  means "no geometry" explicitly rather than "whatever happens to sit on the centre".
- **Two depth slices, not one plane.** The backdrop hangs on a plane normal to the view direction,
  and one plane behind the near geometry would hide the far buildings standing between the camera
  and Wat Ket. Measured: **17,560 of the 61,116 are in front**. Cheap to fix at generation time,
  ugly to retrofit after authoring.
- **`scripts/render-backdrop.ts`** — planned as Python beside `build-region.py`, moved to
  TypeScript once it was clear it needs `lod.ts`, `shading.ts` and `theme.ts`. Mirroring three
  engine modules in another language is precisely the drift everything else here is designed
  against. PNG written by hand for the reason `build-region.py` gives: an image library's output
  varies by version and would destroy byte-identity.

  Greyscale-8, so the byte `getImageData` hands back **is** the tone index — `theme.ts` keeps the
  palette, exactly as it keeps the hypsometric ramp for the relief field. The precedent is the
  16 Sep brand swap: a backdrop with colours baked in would have quietly kept the 1967 PROGRESS
  palette while every other surface moved.

  **61,116 buildings → 547 KB** (386 + 161), 4096 × 2360 px at 0.4163 px/m, 5.8 s, byte-identical
  on a re-run. Rendered both slices through the real palette and looked at them: the old city's
  moat grid, the Ping, temples in civic teal, and the near disc as a clean elliptical hole. The
  two slices tile along a horizontal cut, which is what a constant-depth cut projects to.
- **Sized the raster by VRAM rather than by disk.** 4,096 px looked like the obvious width — the
  PNG is only 386 KB — until the number that actually binds: the browser expands an 8-bit
  greyscale texture to RGBA on upload, so both slices cost **77 MB of video memory at 4,096 and
  19 MB at 2,048**. Looked at the 2,048 render through the real palette before committing to it;
  buildings, roof and wall tones and the disc edge all still read. The projector can have its own
  build via `--width` when there is a projector in the room to judge it on.
- **Closed the staleness hole, which was a real gap in the morning's reasoning.** Asked why the
  backdrop is not simply re-rendered on build. The answer is that "derived rather than authored"
  — the whole reply to the roadmap's objection — only stays true if something re-derives it, and
  a committed artefact goes stale the moment `npm run fetch:osm` rewrites the document. So the
  generator now fingerprints its inputs (every footprint, height, kind and id, the hero set, its
  own parameters) into the sidecar, and a test recomputes it from the committed document.
  Verified by nudging one building 20 cm and watching the suite fail with the message naming the
  fix. Build-time rendering would give the same guarantee; committing keeps the exhibition off
  the critical path of a build step, which is the reason the scene document is committed and the
  Overpass cache is not.
- **Wired the runtime half, and it works.** Schema entry beside `relief`, asset index,
  `BackdropPlane.tsx` hanging the two rasters on quads normal to the view direction, Diorama
  wiring, and `wat-ket.viewer.json` — the same scene with the 61,116 backdrop buildings taken
  out — which `page.tsx` imports instead of the full document.

  | | Before | After |
  |---|---|---|
  | Triangles per frame | ~1.13M | **157,532** |
  | Draw calls | — | **8** |
  | Payload | 4.44 MB gzip | **1.16 MB gzip** |

  Extracting `fetch-osm.ts`'s scene formatter into `scripts/scene-format.ts` was needed the
  moment a second script started writing the document. Checked that `fetch:osm` still writes
  byte-identical output and that the backdrop reference survives a re-import.
- **THE VISUAL VERIFICATION IS UNBLOCKED, and it immediately earned its keep.** Blocked since
  16 Sep because browser automation only reaches a background tab where `visibilityState` is
  `hidden` and `requestAnimationFrame` never fires. Reproduced that exactly — 0 frames in a
  second, canvas stuck at its 300 × 150 default — and then fixed it by focusing the tab with
  AppleScript. rAF starts, the canvas resizes to 3072 × 1223, and the scene renders. The
  debugger slowdown the 19th documented is still there; screenshots work, `Runtime.evaluate`
  times out until the page settles.

  **Three bugs, none of which any test would have caught:**
  1. The entire front slice was invisible — hung just clear of the near set, but the ground it
     depicts runs toward the camera for kilometres and is opaque, so it sat behind all of it.
  2. A full-width horizontal band of missing city either side of the near disc. `sliceFor` sent
     equal-depth buildings BEHIND, on the argument that being wrongly hidden reads as depth. It
     does not; it reads as a hole. And the fear that put them there is groundless — equal-depth
     objects lie on a horizontal screen line *beside* the near disc, never over it.
  3. **The relief backdrop was the largest object in the scene** — 130,050 triangles against the
     near city's 112k. Invisible as a problem until the far city stopped drowning it out.
     Drawing every second cell took it to 32,258, with no refetch of the DEM.

  Also confirmed working while in there: the register crossfade district → region, the
  Valeriepieris circle with its population field and city labels, the caption, and the on-ramp
  handing 2026 over to 2045.
- **The seam passes.** Near geometry blends into the raster with no edge, no ring, no missing
  city; the near buildings read very slightly crisper, which is the resolution tradeoff and not
  a boundary.
- **Left undone**, all recorded in the plan: the pan clamp, the `docs/` updates recording the
  roadmap reversal, and fetching the viewer document as data rather than importing it.

- **Split the one rail into three discrete views, and added the valley between them.** Asked for
  late in the day: the circle and the city "should not be in the same continuum because it's very
  different kinds of renderings", plus a middle view of the valley Chiang Mai and the Ping sit in.
  Both are right, and the second is what the relief field has been hinting at from the corner of
  the frame since the 19th.

  The rail was always paying for the pretence that a 3,437 km population raster and an 8 km
  building diorama are the same kind of thing at different distances. `RELIEF_HOLD_OUT` was the
  clearest tell — it existed only because zooming out shrank the district onto the circle before
  the mountains arrived. `plans/2026-09-21_three-views.plan.md`.

  | View | Triangles | Draw calls |
  |---|---|---|
  | The circle | 68 | 3 |
  | The valley | 130,052 | 2 |
  | Wat Ket | 157,532 | 8 |

  The circle used to carry the whole district through the handover, so the worst case is now one
  view rather than two plus a backdrop. Most of the change was deletion — `RegisterDriver`,
  `ZoomTween`, the crossfade, `districtTransform`, `worldMinZoom` — with only a view gate and a
  camera cut replacing them.
- **The valley field needed `--refresh` and nearly shipped wrong.** The first 120 km run reported
  a peak of 1,675 m and looked plausible; it had silently reused the city backdrop's ±24 km cached
  DEM, so the outer two thirds of the box were sampled from data that did not cover it. The tell
  was that 1,675 m is Doi Suthep, not Doi Inthanon. A refetch pulled all four Copernicus tiles and
  gave 226–2,565 m, and `valley.test.ts` now asserts the peak is above 2,000 m so the same mistake
  cannot pass again.
- **Two more bugs found only by looking**, both from deleting the driver: `RegionPlane`'s materials
  start at `opacity={0}` because the crossfade used to fade them in, so the circle rendered as a
  blank canvas; and `ViewCut` moved the camera to a fixed reach, past near and far planes sized
  for its original position. That is five bugs today that 432 passing tests did not catch.

- **Populated the valley and tried three ways of drawing it.** `scripts/fetch-valley.ts` pulls
  387 named waterways from Overpass over the ±60 km box and reads seven towns out of the GeoNames
  dump `build-region.py` already downloads — no new data dependency. Both render, verified on
  screen: the Ping and its tributaries drawing the basin, and Chiang Mai, Lamphun, San Kamphaeng,
  Hang Dong, San Pa Tong, Pa Sang and Lampang labelled in the DOM over the canvas.
- **The topography styles are half-done, and the honest state is written into the plan.** Three
  are implemented behind `?relief=`: `gradient` (the original), `terraced` (quantised to a contour
  band, flat-faced, three-tone by normal — the project's own rule for buildings applied to
  terrain) and `hillshade` (one colour, north-west light, the map convention).

  **Terraced is implemented but not good.** Two reasons, both now in the code: at 469 m between
  vertices a terrace is often one cell wide, so treads and risers alternate per cell and read as
  confetti rather than contours; and the hypsometric ramp makes harsh jumps across five bands.
  The interval went 100 → 250 → 500 m chasing it. **Hillshade was never seen at all** — the tab
  wedged under the debugger before it could be captured, and it is the one style whose legibility
  does not depend on terrace width.
- **Copernicus GLO-30 is a SURFACE model**, so it carries buildings and tree canopy as 10–40 m of
  jitter per cell. Terracing turned that into static. The field is now box-blurred once before
  anything else touches it — which the gradient style benefits from too.
- **Three perf bugs, all found by the tab freezing rather than by a test.** The valley mesh was
  being built on page load even while the city was on screen — views now build on first visit and
  are kept, which is the whole point of discrete views. `ramp()` was called per face, 130,052
  colour-space conversions per rebuild, now cached per band. And the blur ran twice per render.
- **And one design error the tests caught**: making `valleyHeights` smooth by default coupled pure
  arithmetic to `meta.grid.size` matching the field's length. Smoothing is the caller's job now,
  in one place.

- **Chose the relief style by rendering all three offline and looking at them.** `hillshade`
  wins and is now the default: it reads as a plaster relief model, the basin obviously a flat
  floor between two ranges, ridges and side valleys with real form and no colour doing the work.
  Its base is the city's own Warm White, so the valley and the diorama are the same material at
  different scales.

  **`terraced` lost, and it is worth recording why, because the project's own rules argued for
  it** — quantised bands, flat faces, three tones by face normal, exactly what every building in
  the city view does. At 469 m between vertices a terrace is often one cell wide, so treads and
  risers alternate per cell and the mountains come out as confetti. The argument is still right;
  only the resolution is wrong. Both styles stay behind `?relief=`.
- **Built `scripts/preview-relief.ts` because the browser route failed twice over.** The
  DevTools debugger that drives the page makes a 130k-triangle rebuild take tens of seconds, and
  `screencapture` returns a blank desktop because this environment has no Screen Recording
  permission. The previewer reads the committed field, runs the same pure functions the viewer
  runs, and rasterises them with a z-buffer — so what it shows is what the viewer draws. Three
  styles rendered in a couple of seconds, and the choice took one look.

  **The lesson worth keeping: for anything whose output is an image produced by pure functions,
  rendering it offline beats driving a browser.** The engine was already separated enough to make
  this a sixty-line script.
- Added `?view=` deep links on the way — the exhibition machine opens on a fixed view, and a
  deep link also skips building the city, so opening on the valley no longer extrudes 7,588
  buildings nobody is looking at.
